lesson.menu_title: Things Used to Be Different — Twenty Years of This Industry
lesson.menu_desc: Used to and would, for the way the job worked before everything moved online -- 37 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 8 -- Things Used to Be Different
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rosa M. Mitiko Shida | Lesson 8 -- Things Used to Be Different
lesson.grammar_point: used to and would for past habits

listenings.text: Before we start the training, a short story, because it explains why the system looks the way it does. Twenty years ago there were no corporate portals. Every contract used to arrive on paper, and a courier would bring it to the office twice a week. The account manager used to keep a folder for each client, and if a client called with a question about a fare, she would open the folder and read the answer from a printed page. It sounds slow, and it was. But everybody knew where the paper trail was, and nobody used to lose a contract in a system nobody had access to. That is the part we are still trying to get back.

People ask me what has really changed in this industry in twenty years, and they expect me to say technology. It is not technology. What changed is the amount of time. I used to spend three days a week in front of clients. Three days. I would drive to their office, sit down, drink coffee, and leave two hours later knowing something that was not in any report. Today I have the same number of clients and I see them twice a month, and the rest of the relationship happens on a screen. We used to say that this business was about aircraft. It never was. It used to be about who picked up the phone at six in the evening, and honestly, it still is.

paras: There is a photograph in the Sao Paulo office from about twenty years ago. It shows a wall of shelves, and on the shelves there are folders, one for every corporate client. Nobody under thirty understands what they are looking at.

In those years the job was physical. Contracts used to arrive on paper. A courier would bring them twice a week, and the account manager would file them by hand. If a client called with a question about a fare, she would walk to the shelf, open the folder and read the answer out loud. It was slow, and it was also completely transparent. Everybody knew where the paper trail was.

Then the portals arrived, and with them a promise: everything in one place, available to everybody, instantly. Most of that promise came true. What nobody predicted was the side effect. When the folder was on the shelf, the account manager used to see the whole client every time she opened it. On a screen you see one contract, one route, one invoice, and you have to decide in advance what you are looking for.

The veterans in this industry are not nostalgic about paper, and nobody wants the courier back. What they miss is a habit that the shelf used to force on them. They would look at the whole client, twice a week, whether there was a problem or not. That habit died out quietly, and no system replaced it. The ones who still have it are, without exception, the ones whose clients never leave.
reading.source: Column -- South America Commercial Aviation Review

gist.prompt: What is this column mainly about?
choices: Why companies should go back to paper contracts
A habit the old system forced on people, which no new system replaced

items: The column argues that the old paper system was better than the portals.
The veterans in this industry are not nostalgic about paper, and nobody wants the courier back.
Contracts used to be delivered by a courier twice a week.
A courier would bring them twice a week, and the account manager would file them by hand.
The column says the portals failed to deliver what they promised.
Most of that promise came true.
What the veterans miss is the habit of looking at the whole client regularly.
They would look at the whole client, twice a week, whether there was a problem or not.

items.situation: A younger colleague asks what the job was like when you started.
tips: Used to for a state that is over
Would for an action that repeated

items.situation: Somebody asks why the reporting system is so complicated.
tips: Explain the history in one sentence
It used to be three separate systems, and nobody merged them

items.situation: A client says the service is not what it was.
tips: Agree with the part that is true, then say what replaced it
We used to visit every week -- now we call, and we answer faster

items.situation: You are asked what habit from the old days you would bring back.
tips: Name one, and say what it gave you
I would look at the whole client, not one invoice

items.situation: Somebody asks whether you miss the travel you used to do.
tips: Two halves: what you miss and what you do not
I miss the clients. I do not miss the airport at five in the morning

items.situation: A colleague asks how the corporate contract worked before the portal.
tips: Used to plus base verb for the old routine
It used to arrive on paper, and we would file it by hand

extra_audio.text: Renato says that the photograph on the wall shows the office as it used to be twenty years ago. Rosa asks how the contracts used to arrive before the portal existed. Renato explains that a courier would bring them twice a week and that everything was filed by hand. Rosa asks what he misses most about that way of working. Renato answers that he does not miss the paper, but he misses the habit of looking at the whole client twice a week.
